key_terms.meaning: a_k = (1/N) Σₙ₌₀^{N−1} x[n] e^(−j2πkn/N); the N complex amplitudes that build a period-N sequence
A sequence with x[n] = x[n+N] for all n; the smallest such N is the fundamental period
Which multiple of the fundamental frequency 2π/N a DTFS term sits at; for a period-N sequence only N distinct values of k exist
X(e^(jω)) = Σₙ x[n] e^(−jωn); the continuous, 2π-periodic spectrum of an aperiodic sequence
X(e^(j(ω+2π))) = X(e^(jω)) because e^(−j2πn) = 1 for integer n; the spectrum repeats every 2π rad/sample
Σₙ |x[n]| < ∞; a sufficient condition for the DTFT to exist and be continuous
X[k] = Σₙ₌₀^{N−1} x[n] W_N^{nk}, k = 0, …, N−1; N samples of the DTFT at ω = 2πk/N
W_N = e^(−j2π/N), so W_N^{nk} = e^(−j2πnk/N); the fixed complex number that makes the DFT a matrix product
X(z) = Σₙ₌₋∞^{∞} x[n] z^(−n), a power series in z⁻¹ evaluated at a complex number z
The set of z values for which the z-transform sum converges absolutely; it is part of the transform, not an optional extra
Putting z on the unit circle turns X(z) into the DTFT; the DTFT is the z-transform evaluated on |z| = 1 when the ROC includes the unit circle
x[n − n₀] ↔ z^(−n₀) X(z); the ROC is unchanged except that z = 0 or z = ∞ may be added or removed
x[n] * h[n] ↔ X(z)H(z); the ROC of the product contains the intersection of the two ROCs
aⁿ x[n] ↔ X(z/a); the ROC is scaled by |a|, so poles move radially by the factor a
Writing X(z)/z as a sum of simple terms whose inverse transforms are known geometric sequences
Dividing numerator by denominator to get a series in z⁻¹ or z; the coefficients of the series are the sequence values
A sequence that is zero for n < n₀; its ROC is the region outside the outermost pole, and z = ∞ may be included
H(z) = Y(z)/X(z), the z-transform of the impulse response of an LTI system
Values of z where H(z) → ∞ (roots of the denominator) and where H(z) = 0 (roots of the numerator)
A causal LTI system is stable exactly when all poles of H(z) lie strictly inside the unit circle |z| = 1
H(z) evaluated at z = e^(jω); valid only when the ROC contains the unit circle

takeaways: A period-N sequence carries only N independent complex exponentials, so its DTFS has exactly N distinct coefficients and then repeats.
The DTFT is continuous in ω but always periodic with period 2π, because discrete time makes frequency a wrapped, circular quantity.
The N-point DFT is just the DTFT sampled at ω = 2πk/N, which is why it can be computed as a finite N × N matrix product.
The z-transform is a power series; the algebraic formula alone is incomplete, and the ROC is what pins down the sequence.
Every operation you do in time — shift, scale, convolve, difference — has a one-line z-domain counterpart with a predictable effect on the ROC.
Inverse z-transform is two steps: invert the algebra, then use the ROC to choose causal or anti-causal terms for each pole.
The poles of H(z) relative to the unit circle decide stability and shape the frequency response, without ever solving the difference equation in time.
A causal system is stable only if every pole is strictly inside |z| = 1; a single pole on or outside the circle breaks it.
bank_note: Long answers here almost always reward a correct ROC drawn with the poles, a labelled pole-zero plot, and a clear statement linking pole positions to stability and frequency response.

bank.q: Define the discrete-time Fourier series of a period-N sequence. Write both the analysis and synthesis equations, and explain why the coefficients a_k repeat with period N.
outline: Analysis: a_k = (1/N) Σ over one period of x[n] e^(−j2πkn/N)
Synthesis: x[n] = Σ over one period of a_k e^(j2πkn/N)
Only N distinct exponentials e^(j2πkn/N) exist, since k and k+N give the same exponential
Line spectrum: N spectral lines at ω = 2πk/N

bank.q: Show that the DTFT of any sequence is periodic in ω with period 2π rad/sample. State the condition for the DTFT to exist and give one sequence for which it fails.
outline: Substitute ω + 2π into the defining sum
Use e^(−j2πn) = 1 for integer n
Sufficient condition: Σ|x[n]| < ∞
Example of failure: x[n] = u[n], or a two-sided growing exponential

bank.q: Define the z-transform of a sequence and its region of convergence. Explain with examples why two different sequences can share the same algebraic X(z), and state the ROC rules for right-sided, left-sided and two-sided sequences.
outline: X(z) = Σ x[n] z^(−n), a power series in z⁻¹
ROC = set of z where the sum converges absolutely
Right-sided: outside the outermost pole; left-sided: inside the innermost pole; two-sided: an annulus
Concrete example: aⁿu[n] and −aⁿu[−n−1] give the same X(z) with different ROCs
ROC contains no poles and is a connected region

bank.q: State the time-shift, exponential-scaling, convolution and differentiation properties of the z-transform, and state the ROC in each case.
outline: Shift: x[n−n₀] ↔ z^(−n₀)X(z), ROC unchanged except possibly z = 0 or ∞
Scaling: aⁿx[n] ↔ X(z/a), ROC scaled by |a|
Convolution: x[n]*h[n] ↔ X(z)H(z), ROC contains the intersection
Multiplication by n: n x[n] ↔ −z dX(z)/dz, same ROC
Each ROC statement justified, not just quoted

bank.q: Compute the 4-point DFT of x[n] = {1, 1, 0, 0}. Then write down the DTFT of the same sequence and verify that the four DFT values are samples of it at the correct frequencies.
outline: Use W₄ = −j and the matrix form
DTFT X(e^(jω)) = 1 + e^(−jω)
Sample at ω = 0, π/2, π, 3π/2 and match

bank.q: Find the inverse z-transform of X(z) = z / ((z − 1/2)(z − 1/3)) for the ROC |z| > 1/2. Repeat for |z| < 1/3 and for 1/3 < |z| < 1/2, and identify which case is stable.
outline: Expand X(z)/z into partial fractions to get residues 3 and −2 (or equivalent)
For |z| > 1/2: right-sided terms giving (3(1/2)ⁿ − 2(1/3)ⁿ)u[n]
For |z| < 1/3: left-sided terms, sequence is anti-causal
For 1/3 < |z| < 1/2: two-sided, one term causal and one anti-causal
The middle ROC is the only one containing the unit circle, so only that one corresponds to a stable sequence
Each answer states the ROC explicitly

bank.q: A discrete-time LTI system obeys y[n] − 0.5 y[n−1] = x[n]. Using the z-transform, find H(z), the impulse response, the pole-zero plot, and decide whether the system is stable and causal.
outline: Take z-transforms with the shift property
Pole at z = 0.5, zero at z = 0
Causal ROC |z| > 0.5 gives h[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n]
Pole inside the unit circle, so the causal system is stable
Frequency response H(e^(jω)) = 1/(1 − 0.5 e^(−jω)) is low-pass in shape

bank.q: An LTI system has H(z) = (1 − z⁻¹)/(1 − 0.9 z⁻¹) with ROC |z| > 0.9. Sketch |H(e^(jω))| over 0 ≤ ω ≤ π, mark the value at ω = 0 and ω = π, and describe what the system does to a slowly varying input such as a daily temperature record.
outline: Zero at z = 1 removes d.c., pole near the circle boosts low frequencies
|H| at ω = 0 is zero, at ω = π is about 2/1.9
High-pass character
Slowly varying input is strongly attenuated; fast day-to-day changes pass

bank.q: For the system H(z) = 1/(1 − 1.5 z⁻¹ + 0.5 z⁻²), find all possible ROCs, give the impulse response for each, and say which ROC gives a stable system and which gives a causal one.
outline: Factor the denominator into poles at z = 1 and z = 0.5
Partial fractions give terms (1)ⁿ and (0.5)ⁿ with signs chosen by the ROC
|z| > 1 is causal but unstable (pole on the unit circle)
0.5 < |z| < 1 is stable but non-causal

bank.q: Compare the DTFS, DTFT, DFT and z-transform in a table covering: the class of signal each applies to, whether the resulting description is discrete or continuous, finite or infinite, and periodic or not. Explain how one reduces to another in the appropriate limit.
outline: DTFS: periodic discrete signal, N discrete coefficients, periodic in k
DTFT: aperiodic discrete signal, continuous 2π-periodic in ω
DFT: finite-length discrete signal, N discrete coefficients, implicitly periodic
z-transform: any sequence, function of a complex variable with an ROC
DFT = DTFT sampled at ω = 2πk/N; DTFT = z-transform on |z| = 1; DTFS coefficients are samples of one period of the DTFT of one period of the sequence
Correct statements about circular versus linear interpretation

bank.q: Two LTI systems with transfer functions H₁(z) and H₂(z) are connected in cascade. Discuss the ROC of the overall transfer function, what happens to the frequency response if a pole of H₁ cancels a zero of H₂, and whether such cancellations are safe in a real implementation.
outline: Overall H(z) = H₁(z)H₂(z)
ROC contains the intersection of the two ROCs
Pole-zero cancellation changes the algebraic expression but the physical response can still be excited by initial conditions or by numerical error
An unstable pole cancelled by a zero leaves an internally unstable system even though the input-output description looks fine
Practical answer: cascade is safe when each block is separately stable, and pole-zero cancellation near the unit circle should be avoided

bank.q: A second-order causal system has poles at z = r e^(±jθ) with 0 < r < 1. Derive its impulse response and frequency response, and discuss how r and θ set the decay rate, the ringing frequency and the resonant peak. Choose r and θ for a system that must ring at about one-tenth of the sampling rate and settle within about fifty samples.
outline: h[n] is rⁿ times a sinusoid at θ, damped geometric decay
Decay time constant set by r: larger r means slower decay, sharper resonance
θ sets the ringing frequency in rad/sample
Resonant peak near ω = θ, height roughly controlled by 1/(1 − r)
r ≈ 0.9 gives settling in a few tens of samples; θ = 2π/10 gives one cycle in ten samples
State that the system is stable for any r < 1 and conditionally stable behaviour at r = 1

bank.q: You record 1024 samples of a vibration signal and compute its DFT. Explain how zero padding, windowing and the choice of record length change what you see, and why two engineers using different record lengths may report different peak frequencies for the same machine.
outline: DFT samples the DTFT at 2πk/N: longer records give finer spacing
Zero padding interpolates the same underlying spectrum, it does not add resolution
Resolution is set by the observation time, roughly 1/T in Hz
Rectangular window causes leakage; tapering windows trade main-lobe width for sidelobe level
Spectral leakage can move the apparent peak and hide a small tone next to a large one
Implicit periodicity of the DFT means a non-integer number of cycles in the record creates a discontinuity

bank.q: Explain deconvolution using the z-transform. Given Y(z) = H(z)X(z), discuss when the inverse system 1/H(z) is causal and stable, and what happens when H(z) has zeros on or outside the unit circle.
outline: Inverse system has transfer function 1/H(z): poles of the inverse are the zeros of H
Causal and stable inverse requires all zeros of H inside the unit circle (minimum-phase system)
Zeros outside the circle give a stable inverse only if it is allowed to be non-causal
Zeros exactly on the circle make the inverse unstable or undefined at that frequency
Practical consequence: noise at frequencies where |H| is small is amplified

glossary.def: The representation of a periodic discrete-time sequence as a finite sum of N complex exponentials.
The representation of an aperiodic sequence as a continuous, 2π-periodic function of frequency ω.
An N-point transform that maps N time samples to N frequency samples equally spaced over one full 2π turn.
The power series X(z) = Σ x[n] z^(−n) that generalises the DTFT to complex values of z.
The set of complex z values for which the z-transform sum converges absolutely.
A value of z at which the transfer function or transform becomes infinite.
A value of z at which the numerator, and hence the transform, equals zero.
The set |z| = 1 in the z-plane; on it the z-transform becomes the DTFT.
The constant W_N = e^(−j2π/N) raised to integer powers inside the DFT sum.
The convolution of two periodic sequences taken over one period; it is what multiplication of DFTs corresponds to.
The ordinary convolution sum of two aperiodic sequences, equal to circular convolution when the period is long enough.
A sequence that is zero for all negative values of n.
A sequence that is zero for n less than some finite index, not necessarily zero.
Property that the sum of the magnitudes of the sequence terms is finite.
A way of writing a rational transform as a sum of simple fractions whose inverse transforms are known.
The z-transform of the impulse response of an LTI system; it equals Y(z)/X(z) for zero initial conditions.
The complex gain H(e^(jω)) that an LTI system applies to a complex exponential input at frequency ω.
A relation expressing the present output sample in terms of past outputs and present and past inputs.
The property that every bounded input produces a bounded output; for causal z-transforms it means all poles inside the unit circle.
A causal, stable system whose zeros also all lie inside the unit circle, so a causal stable inverse exists.
The spreading of energy from one frequency bin into neighbouring bins when the record length is not an integer number of periods.
Appending zeros to a finite record before the DFT, which interpolates the spectrum without improving resolution.
